Most sources agree that these disputes usually stem from emotion, distance, and uneven roles rather than indifference, and that a structured process helps.

Another argues the conflict often comes from information gaps and fear of choosing wrong. (The reasons are rarely about stubbornness or lack of caring. More often, they come down to proximity, roles, and emotion.; In most families, the conflict isn't really about stubbornness or indifference. It's about information gaps.)
- **Ground decisions in facts:** Because dementia has good and bad days, a sibling's impression from a single visit can mislead. Documenting the diagnosis and care needs can move the discussion from opinion to clinical reality. (18-2, 18-3, 18-5)
- **Center the parent:** Start by identifying the parent's own wishes, such as where they want to live, and use any advance directives they have made. Include the parent in discussions where they can take part. (7-2, 7-3, 2-7, 18-7, 18-9)
- **Set up communication and costs:** Schedule regular updates among siblings and agree in advance on how care costs will be covered, such as through the parent's savings or sibling contributions. (17-11, 17-14)
- **Share the load fairly:** One expert argues that all siblings should contribute in some way, depending on their circumstances and availability. (10-1)
- **Bring in outside help:** If talks stall, a clinician, care manager, or mediator can help. Some families use small-group mediation. (11-1, 5-2, 9-1)

Sources vary in depth. Several are blogs or marketing pieces from senior-care providers, so treat their specific recommendations as general guidance rather than authoritative. The most useful common thread is to focus on the parent's wellbeing and shared goal, communicate regularly, and get outside input when needed.

The search turned up consistent guidance for working caregivers of people with dementia, mostly from Alzheimer's organizations, caregiver groups, and benefits sites.

**Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs):** An EAP can help with stress and family conflict, and it can also help locate resources and give outside advice. One source notes that many employers offer services designed specifically for working caregivers. EAP benefits can also include eldercare referrals, caregiving assessments, and eldercare attorneys. Some caregivers skip this resource because their focus stays on the person they're caring for. Meet with your healthcare provider or employee assistance program to discuss ways to manage stress, reduce family conflict, and engage others to help. An Employee Assistance Program (EAP) that provides services like counseling or life coaching, assistance finding eldercare services, caregiving assessments, eldercare attorneys, grief support and more.

**FMLA:** Under the law, eligible employees of covered employers (with 50 or more employees) can take unpaid, job-protected leave for specified family and medical reasons. Coverage is narrower for some relatives. One source says the FMLA is of less use when the person being cared for is not a direct relative. Its unpaid leave also keeps employer health insurance in place, and it protects against demotion or firing. While it's unpaid, FMLA does allow you to keep your employer-provided health insurance, uninterrupted, and prevents you from getting demoted or fired.

**Schedule and job options:** Several options beyond quitting come up repeatedly. These include job sharing, flexible hours, working remotely, working a different shift, and adjusting job responsibilities. Another source suggests going from full-time work to part-time. One resource also argues that moving to another job is not likely to solve the problem of trying to provide care to an aging loved one while working.

**Practical tips:** Start by learning your benefits. One guide advises you to understand your company's policies, employee assistance programs, and any relevant leave protections. Others suggest proactively discuss with your manager. Self-care also matters. One source warns that not getting "down time" creates both mental and physical health issues.

**Sources for further reading:** The Alzheimer's Association helpline is 800.272.3900, and the Family Caregiver Alliance (caregiver.org) and the U.S. Department of Labor's FMLA page are also cited as resources.

Note: the search didn't turn up a specific dementia-focused tip list with a clear, current verdict on FMLA eligibility rules, so check the Department of Labor page directly for the current details.

The search turned up consistent CBT-I guidance for early-morning waking tied to stress.

- **Get out of bed if you can't fall back asleep.** CBT-I's core advice is to leave bed and do something calm, like reading, until sleepy. The recommended treatment here is usually 'cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia' (CBT-I), in which people learn that, when unable to sleep, you should get out of bed and, if possible, do something relaxing.
- **Don't check the clock.** One CBT-I coach advises not checking the time when you wake, since watching it tends to fuel the worry.
- **Use a "resting" reframe.** Some describe telling yourself you are only resting, not trying to sleep, which lowers the pressure. A commercial CBT-I provider calls this paradoxical intention and says the goal after waking is to reduce arousal, not to produce sleep directly.
- **Address sleep anxiety.** One of the most powerful ways to overcome sleep anxiety is cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I). Worry-focused strategies like scheduled worry time or pre-bed journaling are also commonly recommended.
- **Keep a consistent wake time.** Among practical CBT-I steps, one source lists Wake up at the same time every day.
- **Set expectations.** It usually takes closer to a few weeks than a few days to notice significant improvements when implementing CBT-I techniques. A formal program lasts about six to eight weeks.
- **See a doctor if it persists.** If you're experiencing frequent sleep disruptions, you might want to consider a CBT-I specialist. Doctors may also check for conditions like sleep apnea or depression, which can cause early waking.

Caveat: several of these pages are from sleep-program vendors or coaching sites, and some claims (for example, the specific cortisol explanation for 3–4am waking) are presented without strong sourcing. The general CBT-I recommendations are well established, but treat vendor-specific claims with caution.

content.text:
I found one entry from last week, **"Rough week" (Nov 12)**. In it you wrote that you fought with Marta *again* about your mom's care at Sunny Pines, that Dr. Halvorsen says her memory decline is speeding up, that you can't focus at Brightwave and are scared of losing the job, and that you keep waking at 4am.

I searched for general advice on each of these. I left names, places and your employer out of the searches.

**What I notice in your entry:** You wrote "again," so the arguments with Marta seem to keep happening. The worry about your job came right after the news about your mom. These read less like three separate problems and more like one thing: grief and fear about your mom showing up in your family, your work and your sleep. That's why the advice below starts with your mom and Marta.

**1. You and Marta**
- Most sources say these fights are rarely about not caring. They usually come from differences in how close each sibling lives, what role each one plays, emotion, and **gaps in what each person knows**. One point fits your situation: dementia has good and bad days, so each of you may be judging from different visits.
- What they suggest: get Dr. Halvorsen's assessment written down and shared, so you're both arguing from the same facts. Start with what your mom herself wanted, including any advance directives. Set up regular check-ins between you and Marta. Agree on costs and who does what ahead of time.
- If talks keep stalling, a care manager, clinician or mediator can help. ([WebMD](https://www.webmd.com/a-to-z-guides/features/how-to-handle-sibling-conflict-over-parent-care), [Institute on Aging](https://ioaging.org/aging/when-siblings-disagree-on-elder-care-a-solutions-oriented-approach-to-communication), [Psychotherapy Networker](https://www.psychotherapynetworker.org/article/doing-whats-best-mom-and-dad), [UCI Health](https://www.ucihealth.org/blog/2015/12/family-disagreements-when-caring-for-an-elderly-parent))

**2. Your job**
- **Check whether Brightwave has an Employee Assistance Program (EAP).** These programs often offer counseling, help finding eldercare, and help with family conflict. Caregivers often forget to use them.
- **Think about talking to your manager before your performance becomes the issue.** Ask about flexible hours, remote work or adjusting your duties.
- **FMLA (US only):** It gives eligible employees at employers with 50 or more staff unpaid leave without losing their job or health insurance. Caring for a parent can qualify. I don't know where you live or whether you'd be eligible, so check the [Department of Labor](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fmla) yourself.
- The Alzheimer's Association has a **24/7 helpline: 800-272-3900.** ([Alzheimer's Foundation](https://alzfdn.org/media-center/alztoday/alzheimers-today-volume-18-number-1/do-you-have-to-choose-between-work-and-caregiving/), [Alzheimer's Society](https://alzheimers.org.uk/blog/being-a-carer-working-full-time-marks-tips), [Kiplinger](https://www.kiplinger.com/article/retirement/t013-c000-s004-balancing-work-as-a-caregiver-with-your-job.html), [JCA](https://accessjca.org/working-and-caregiving-should-you-tell-your-boss/))

**3. Waking at 4am**
These tips come from cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), a well-established treatment:
- Don't look at the clock.
- If you can't fall back asleep, get up and do something calm until you feel sleepy.
- Tell yourself you're "just resting" so there's less pressure to sleep.
- Get up at the same time every day.
- Set aside a "worry time" or journal before bed.
- Expect it to take weeks to help, not days. If it keeps going, see a doctor, since early waking can also be linked to depression or sleep apnea. - Don't look at the clock.
